newsitem.title: UK: London gold touch easier, palladium flourishes.
newsitem.headline: London gold touch easier, palladium flourishes.

text.p: Palladium took centre stage in otherwise quiet precious metals markets on Wednesday after Tokyo went limit up on short covering, traders said.
Palladium fixed at $208.00 per ounce, $10.00 above its Tuesday fixing and its highest level since June 12.
Its sister metal platinum fixed a dollar firmer at $426.00 while gold edged back 15 cents at its 0930 GMT fixing to $326.40
"They are all pretty quiet this morning with gold looking to be locked into a $324-$328 range," one dealer said, adding that the exception was palladium, which was showing signs of going higher.
"There has been significant fund buying. They look like they are trying to take on the Russians," he added.
Palladium has risen in a near-straight line rise since it dropped from a 17-year peak of $240.00 on June 6 to a low of $162.00 on July 10, and the advance accelerated overnight.

"Palladium futures went limit up on Tocom as Japanese investors scrambled to cover short positions. It looks like they did not get that resolved in one day. They will try again tomorrow so this is no time to go short," a dealer said.

The firmer tone in platinum and palladium comes after Russia, the leading exporter of palladium and second biggest shipper of platinum, began shipping to Japan this month for the first time since 1996.
Administrative problems were blamed for the delay, which tightened the markets to a near standstill and sent borrowing rates soaring.
Russia's Almazjuvelirexport agency has been offering spot parcels of palladium for Zurich delivery in Europe since last Friday and has been writing business, dealers said.
However, deliveries are not due until early August, which has brought a rash of borrowing to hedge the purchases between order and delivery date, they said.
This has contributed to keeping borrow rates at levels between 60-80 percent for up to a month.
Dealers are believed to have been looking for discounts against cash prices to cover the high cost of financing the purchases, dealers said.
"When the Russians started offering sizeable lots, I thought the price would go down, but it hasn't. It'll be interesting to see what happens when the metal begins to arrive," one said.
Platinum was at $425.00/$428.00, unchanged, and silver was two cents firmer at $4.34/$4.36.
